title: Medieval Christian scholars called a Muslim judge from Córdoba simply ‘the Commentator’

cover.alt: A white stone statue of Averroes, seated in a robe and turban with a book on his knee, on a granite plinth in front of Córdoba’s crenellated medieval wall.

body: Ibn Rushd, known in Latin as Averroes, was born in Córdoba in 1126 and worked as a judge and a court physician as well as a philosopher, writing more than 100 books. He wrote commentaries on nearly all of Aristotle’s surviving works, and through them Latin Europe learned to read Aristotle. Christian writers referred to him not by name but simply as ‘the Commentator’. Thomas Aquinas relied heavily on his reading of Aristotle while disagreeing with him on many points, and his ideas were controversial enough that the Church condemned them in 1270 and 1277. In the Islamic world, by contrast, his influence stayed modest until modern times.

slides.prompt: Dante gave Averroes a place in the Divine Comedy. Where did he put him?
slides.answer: In the first circle of hell
slides.detail: Dante describes him as the one ‘who made the Great Commentary’: even a Christian poet identified him by his commentary on Aristotle.

slides.question: Raphael painted Averroes into The School of Athens. Where is he?
slides.explanation: He wears a green robe and a turban and peers out from behind Pythagoras.
